name: Tomas Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a plastic-film extruder and check thickness across the roll before it is wrapped. I have a vocational machine certificate and years on the line, but I am an experienced mid-level operator, about average at the job. I like a smooth edge that needs no argument at the packing table.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and how do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Mira works at a pharmacy and our grown children have moved out. We pay a house loan, I earn the usual operator wage, have about three months of expenses saved, and there are some other plants nearby. I use AI now and then to tidy shift notes, but I compare it with the gauge sheet before recording anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the film plant that little software gains are fine if the rolls still meet thickness limits. I am the one who feels the edge of a finished roll before the wrapper closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Mira works in a pharmacy, our grown children have moved out, and we still pay for the house. My pay is ordinary for an extruder operator and we have about three months saved; a small AI saving does not change the monthly arithmetic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the extrusion shift and log each thickness reading. I sometimes use AI to tidy my shift notes, but I would compare the result with the gauge sheet; I would also transfer a set amount from each fresh full pay packet toward the house loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the work staying familiar. There is time to take Mira to the market on Saturday without treating every new screen as a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why feel the edge?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A raised lip can tear the next roll in packing, even when the centre gauge looks fine. I mark it before the wrapper hides it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does AI set the extruder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it only helps me sort occasional notes. The gauge and the written setup sheet govern the machine.

I would accept **small paperwork savings** without changing the safe setup.
think: Our **three-month reserve** covers a brief interruption, not years.
Mira’s **pharmacy wage** and my typical pay cover current bills.
do: Keep **film extrusion shifts** and check roll edges.
Compare **occasional AI notes** with the gauge sheet.
Pay extra **house-loan principal** from fresh full wages.
feel: **Calm** about stable work and the current household budget.

fieldNote: His **vocational certificate** and long experience support average mid-level machine skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office can improve ordering first, but a robot working near hot film needs more patience. If the plant shows us a better thickness chart, I will try it after someone explains the readings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can imagine fewer people on the packing end once robots spread, though extrusion itself still needs watching. Losing even a few paid shifts would press our loan, and the other nearby plants have only some openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor for an offered paid classroom slot to learn the new AI thickness chart using old batches, then check its alerts against the gauge with the senior setter. I would keep making film; if paid hours actually fall, I would apply for posted reachable operator jobs only where pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the rota, but willing to test a chart that another operator has checked first. A coloured warning is not a measurement until we match it to the film.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes the chart safe to try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old batches, a paid lesson and a senior setter beside me. I would not change a live temperature setting because a screen flashed red.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell about reduced hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira first, so we could price the loan and travel together. A factory posting only helps if the wage works after getting there.

I would keep **physical film checks** beside any screen alert.
think: Robot packing could reduce **my paid shifts** on the extrusion line.

feel: **Anxious** about plausible shift cuts, yet open to tested instruction.

fieldNote: He takes **new AI chart learning** only after a real paid lesson with prior batches and supervision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AGI arrives in 2028 when I am sixty, and capable film-handling robots around 2031 when I am sixty-three. The production planner changes before the rolls move themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a robot-run extrusion line to take most of my paid shift when the plant rebuilds it. Mira’s pharmacy wage and three months saved are not enough to carry the house loan for long, and some local factories may be changing too; I would lie awake over the next instalment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask our union delegate for a written rebuild timetable and shift terms, and postpone replacing the family car. I would search posted reachable operator and stockroom roles now, applying only where net pay after travel covers housing and food; I would not quit an existing shift before an actual offer and start date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed about a large wage loss. A roll can wait on a rack, but a loan payment has a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a guess. I would need actual retirement income and house-loan figures that cover essentials before leaving paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children help with the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I could ask for a ride to an interview, but I would not budget their pay as ours.

say: I would ask for **written rebuild terms** before robots arrive.
I would tell the family **2031 physical work** is the sharper shift risk.
think: I expect **most paid shifts** to disappear with the robot wrapper.
Our **three-month reserve** and Mira’s wage cannot carry the loan for long.
do: Request **written rebuild timetable** and shift terms through the union.
Postpone **family car replacement** to protect the house budget.
Apply for **posted reachable jobs** only at bill-covering net pay before quitting.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over expected major wage loss.
S2.quote: A roll can wait on a rack, but a loan payment has a date.
fieldNote: His **expected shift loss** and loan exposure support alarm despite a second household wage.
The **early job search** requires posted work, adequate net pay, a real offer and start date before resignation.

steps.text: Request written rebuild timetable and shift terms through union delegate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AGI reaches the planning desk in 2031 when I am sixty-three, and capable robots reach the rolls around 2034 when I am sixty-six. Five years could be used to train people who know the material.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like to move into film-quality testing, but I cannot pay course fees or lose shifts while learning. A certificate matters only if a reachable plant has posted work that pays enough after travel, and my present role still needs the house loan paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid extrusion shift and ask the employer and union for a funded paid-time quality course. If I am offered a real place with supervised safe sampling on an isolated machine and a posted reachable quality role at bill-covering net pay, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for that role, or check posted operator openings if no course place comes and hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious but able to make a measured choice while paid time remains. I would rather cut a sample beside a qualified tester than buy a certificate from a leaflet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A qualified tester would show me how to cut and measure a film strip with the machine stopped. I would need the offered paid place before touching the sampler.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the old AI notes for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps for organising results, as I do now. They do not teach the physical sampling skill or give me a quality certificate.

say: I would seek **paid quality instruction** for operators who know film.
I would ask for **posted quality wages** before enrolling.
think: An **unpaid course** would hurt the loan budget and take away shifts.
My **material knowledge** helps only with recognised supervised practice.
do: Enrol in **funded quality course** only with offered paid safe practice and adequate posted work.
Apply after **qualification** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay quality role.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to compare a real course and job.

fieldNote: He is **steady with technology** but requires a recognised paid practical route before changing trades.
The **later application** needs offered funded safe instruction and a posted reachable role with enough net income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the family that thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight and robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years is useful for sorting the mortgage and our actual retirement numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had pictured leaving full-time shifts at sixty-seven, but a three-month reserve is not retirement income. Mira’s future wage, any pension and the remaining loan must be priced rather than guessed, and our grown children are building their own lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the extrusion shift and pay extra house-loan principal from fresh full wages after bills. I would request retirement and loan figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would leave the factory then, but if not I would continue safe paid work, and in the first year after 2036 I would check posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about the distant robot line but okay about present earnings. I want a last shift chosen from a household budget, not a date printed on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your hands make the line difficult?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare lighter posted jobs and their actual wages after travel. I would not count a pension before seeing what it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children join the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, their households are separate. I would explain our plan to them, but not assign them our loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because film-handling robots around 2031 could remove most of my shifts while the loan still needs payment. Written rebuilding dates, a funded paid safe course, and posted reachable work with enough pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask which sheet of film the chart was checked against. I trust a measured strip more than a green box on a screen, even if the box sometimes helps me find a mistake.

headlineQuote: I trust a measured strip more than a green box on a screen, even if the box sometimes helps me find a mistake.
portrait: **Tomas**, 58, is an experienced mid-level film extruder operator with a vocational certificate and average line skill.
He has **typical pay**, pharmacy-worker partner Mira, grown children, a house loan, three months saved and some nearby plants.
He uses **AI occasionally** for notes and would learn a new quality chart only through offered paid supervised practice.
Expected **2031 shift cuts** alarm him; a planned age-sixty-seven exit requires verified income for household essentials.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because 2031 robots may remove most paid extrusion shifts while the house loan remains.
whatWouldHelp: **Written rebuild dates**, funded paid safe instruction and posted reachable work with bill-covering net pay would help.
